messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 77-year-old married man and long-time delivery driver, has been struggling with the aftermath of an assault that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event was sudden and vicious: while making his rounds on a quiet evening street, he was ambushed by a masked assailant who attacked him without warning. John had come to believe that such violence would never happen in his neighborhood or during one of his routine deliveries. This unexpected attack shattered his sense of security and control over his environment. Since the assault, John has been plagued by intense feelings of self-doubt and confusion about how he should respond to everyday situations. He often finds himself questioning whether he will do the right thing, particularly when faced with choices that might put him in a vulnerable position again. This constant uncertainty leads him to work excessively hard at keeping busy with other tasks to distract himself from these intrusive thoughts. John had come to believe that if he thinks about the event too much, he will not be able to handle it. This belief has led him to suppress his thoughts and memories of the assault through various maladaptive strategies. One such strategy is overeating; John often finds himself reaching for food as a way to manage his distress. The more he indulges in eating excessively, the less control he feels he has over his life, which only reinforces his self-doubt. The trauma has also affected his work as a delivery driver. John’s occupation requires him to navigate unfamiliar and sometimes isolated areas, making it challenging for him to avoid places that trigger flashbacks or feelings of vulnerability. He tries to keep himself busy with deliveries to avoid thinking about the assault, but this busyness often leaves him exhausted and further distracts from his emotional well-being. John’s marriage has also been impacted by these struggles. His wife notices changes in John’s behavior and is concerned about how he isolates himself when they are at home. Despite her support, John feels like he cannot fully trust that he will do the right thing to keep their family safe or to handle his own emotions effectively. The incident has left John with a sense of shattered beliefs about the world around him. He no longer trusts that his environment is safe and secure, which makes it difficult for him to engage in activities outside of work without feeling anxious. This anxiety further fuels his overeating and excessive busyness as ways to cope with his internal turmoil. John’s most recent encounter with these overwhelming emotions occurred when he was driving past the street where the assault took place. The trigger brought back vivid memories, leading to a surge of distress that he tried to suppress through increased eating and working longer hours than usual. This cycle has left him feeling physically drained and emotionally exhausted. It is this constant state of emotional strain and his growing sense that he cannot manage his thoughts and feelings effectively that finally pushed John to seek help. He hopes to regain control over his life and find healthier ways to cope with the trauma without relying on maladaptive strategies like overeating or busyness. What frightens him most is the fear of being unable to protect himself and his loved ones, but he remains hopeful for a future where these fears no longer dominate his daily existence.
